clue.text: Violent act, a bit like pancake mix?

parts.note: pancakes are made from a runny flour-egg-milk mix called batter
the suffix -y turns a noun into an adjective meaning somewhat like it, as in milky

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether an act of violence resembles pancake batter.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful reading: something batter-like would be battery, just as something like milk is milky.
explanation.definitionFit: Battery is the legal term for unlawful physical force against a person, as in the phrase assault and battery.

clue.text: Preacher of letters overwhelmed by beer

indicators.note: to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so one piece is swallowed up inside another

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
letters arriving by mail are the post

explanation.surface: A preacher who writes letters is drowned out by drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' tempts you towards the alphabet, but here it means mail. The New Testament apostles, like Paul, were also famous letter writers.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is one of the early Christian missionaries sent out to spread the gospel by preaching.

clue.text: Fly northwards with love and dance

indicators.note: in a down entry, heading north means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a gnat is a small fly
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: An instruction to fly north with a lover and dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' reads as a verb but is the insect. Love as O comes from the tennis score.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance originating in Argentina, so it is a specific example of a dance.

clue.text: Chairs for 27 rivals

definitions.meaning: first meaning: chairs on curved runners that rock back and forth
second meaning: the leather-jacketed motorbike gang who fought the scooter riders of the cross-referenced clue

explanation.surface: Seating arranged for a group of competing opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 across is MODS. Mods and Rockers were rival British youth subcultures of the 1960s: Mods rode scooters, Rockers rode motorbikes, and they clashed at seaside towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocking chairs are often just called rockers, while the Rockers were the biker gang famously opposed to the Mods.

clue.text: Looked into dust storm, initially in equatorial desert

indicators.note: a storm whirls things about, so these letters are blown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of each following word counts

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone peered into a dust storm somewhere in a desert near the equator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dust storm' looks like a single weather phrase, but the storm is what scrambles the dust.
explanation.definitionFit: To have studied something is to have examined or investigated it closely, a direct synonym for looked into.

clue.text: Skipping school, tour USA (North-West's borders)

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, as in 'he was truant'

indicators.note: the borders of something are its edges, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of this word
the first and last letters of this abbreviation
the first and last letters of the hyphenated compass point

explanation.surface: A pupil bunks off school to tour the American North-West.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket seems to tell you which region of the USA to tour, but 'borders' applies to all three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant is a pupil absent from lessons without permission, so being truant means skipping school.

clue.text: Multiple events, then a cold snap

indicators.note: to snap is to break, and broken letters are put back together in another order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A run of incidents is followed by a sudden spell of cold weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold snap' reads as a weather phrase, splitting the anagram indicator from its fodder in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The decathlon is an athletics competition made up of ten separate track and field disciplines, hence multiple events.

clue.text: Some of the clientele mentioned water, perhaps

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are wanted, a run lying across the words

parts.note: found spanning the end of the second word and start of the third

explanation.surface: A few customers asked for water.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the tail of 'clientele' into 'mentioned'. 'Perhaps' signals that water is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: In the classical scheme of earth, air, fire and water, water is one of the four elements.

clue.text: For spies into mischief infiltrated by 'one taking orders', in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: to be infiltrated is to have something slip inside, so one piece is placed within the rest

parts.note: pro means in favour of, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: mischief causes disorder, so the letters it acts on are jumbled

parts.note: the CIA is the American intelligence agency
taken as written, to be rearranged
a nun has taken holy orders

explanation.surface: Spies cause mischief after being penetrated by an agent who obeys commands, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One taking orders' sounds like a junior agent, but taking holy orders is what a nun does. The nun slips in just after the opening chunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronunciation is the way in which words are sounded out, which is a manner or style of speaking.

clue.text: Blue feathers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sad, low in spirits
second meaning: the soft fine plumage of birds, used in pillows

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a description of a bird's colour; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down means feeling depressed, and down is also the fluffy layer of plumage stuffed into quilts.

clue.text: Boils spuds or pasta for relative to tuck into

indicators.note: tucking into food means eating it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: potatoes and pasta are starchy foods, or carbohydrates
an uncle is a family relative

explanation.surface: Someone boils potatoes or pasta for a family member to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boils' looks like a cooking verb, but it is the noun for skin infections. Spuds is British slang for potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbuncle is a large painful skin abscess, essentially a cluster of linked boils, so the plural noun matches.

clue.text: In hotel, gripped by a book

indicators.note: to be gripped is to be held tight, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a tome is a large book
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone in a hotel is absorbed in a gripping book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In hotel' reads as a location, but 'In' alone is the definition. A gripping book is also the surface joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in, as in not out of the house, means being at home and available to callers.

clue.text: Hugo Boss announcing no neckwear for a decade

indicators.note: a German fashion house speaking says the next word in German and out loud, so we want how it sounds

parts.note: nein is German for no and sounds like the number
ties are worn round the neck

explanation.surface: A menswear brand declares ties are out for the next ten years.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugo Boss is a German label, which tells you to say 'no' in German. Only that word is sounded; the neckwear is taken straight.
explanation.definitionFit: The nineties is the ten-year period from 1990 to 1999, so it names one particular decade.

clue.text: Changing direction, vicar? Hesitate, then sign off

parts.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a vicar's title

indicators.note: something off is out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: er is the sound of hesitating
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A vicar changes his mind, pauses, then signs off a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign off' looks like a phrase meaning to finish, but 'off' acts on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Reversing a car, or a decision, means going backwards and so turning to the opposite way.

clue.text: Viewer plugged in here

parts.note: surface reading: a television set connected to a wall outlet
setter's reading: the viewer is the organ of sight, set into a hollow in the skull

explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewer' suggests a TV or a person watching one; it is really the organ you watch with, and its socket is anatomical.
explanation.definitionFit: The bony cavity in the skull that holds the eyeball is called the orbit, or more casually its socket.

clue.text: Glamour of biker escaping blitzkrieg, somehow

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the remaining letters are put together in another order
whatever escapes gets out and is gone, so those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, these letters to be removed

explanation.surface: The romance of a motorcyclist fleeing a wartime bombardment.
explanation.walkthrough: The biker's letters are scattered through the long word, not a solid block; once removed, five letters remain to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Glitz is showy, superficial glamour, a close informal synonym associated with show business.

clue.text: Card acceptable in one half of Jersey

indicators.note: keeping just one half means the other half is discarded
in places one piece within the other

parts.note: deleting the second half of the six letters leaves the first three
OK means acceptable

explanation.surface: A credit card is accepted on one side of the island of Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey is a Channel Island off the French coast, but here it is just a word to be halved.
explanation.definitionFit: The joker is the extra playing card in a pack, often wild, so it is one kind of card.

clue.text: Not quite honoured, playing for 60 minutes

indicators.note: not quite all means falling just short, so the final letter is dropped
playing about with something rearranges it, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A player not quite given full honours after an hour on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing for 60 minutes' paints a sports match, but 'playing' acts on the shortened word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sixty minutes make up exactly one hour, a straightforward equivalent measurement of time.

clue.text: Lean to one side and sneer, agitating the audience

parts.note: a ship lists when it leans over

indicators.note: to agitate is to stir up, so these letters are churned into another order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A performer leans over and sneers, stirring up the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agitating the audience' reads as one phrase, but 'agitating' works on the word before it and 'the audience' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience at a concert or broadcast consists of the people who hear it, so they are listeners.

clue.text: Shine like the seafood in Yorkshire?

parts.note: in Yorkshire dialect the word is clipped to t', as in 'down t'pit'
a winkle is a small edible sea snail

explanation.surface: A question about whether to shine like a Yorkshire shellfish dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire speech famously shortens 'the' to t', so 'the winkle' becomes t'winkle. The question mark flags the dialect trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To twinkle is to sparkle or glitter with flickering light, as stars do, so it is a synonym for shine.

clue.text: What's left of rise may be owing

indicators.note: may be suggests what the letters could turn into, a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
money owing is due

explanation.surface: Whatever remains of a pay rise might be owed to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests leftover money, but 'of' just links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A residue is the remainder of something after the main part has been removed or used up.

clue.text: Cat eating a rat's head? Speak with it!

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a lynx is a wild cat
taken as written

indicators.note: the head is the top or front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the rodent

explanation.surface: A cat is devouring a rat's head, and the clue dares you to talk with that.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole exclamation: the thing you speak with. 'Head' looks like part of the rat's body being eaten, but it picks out one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The larynx, or voice box, holds the vocal cords that vibrate to produce speech.

clue.text: Vibrant tirade about broken nose

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: a rant is an angry tirade

indicators.note: something broken comes apart and is reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lively outburst about someone's fractured nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken nose' looks like an injury, but 'broken' rearranges the word, and the rant wraps round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A resonant voice or sound is deep, full and reverberating, which is the sense of vibrant here.

clue.text: Mind check and vacate the set after Matilda stands in line, they say

parts.note: Matilda is the setter, who refers to herself as I

indicators.note: they say points to what people speak, so we want the sound rather than the spelling

parts.note: to stand in line is to queue, which sounds like the letter

indicators.note: to vacate is to empty, so the insides go and only the outside letters stay

parts.note: the first and last letters of this word
the first and last letters of this word

explanation.surface: Clearing a film set after the setter joins the queue, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Matilda is this puzzle's setter, so her name stands for I. 'Vacate the set' sounds like leaving a stage, but it empties both words.
explanation.definitionFit: An IQ test measures intelligence quotient, so it is an examination of mental ability, a check on the mind.

clue.text: Newspaper getting by

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a London daily paper, named with the definite article
second meaning: multiplied by, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A newspaper just about scraping by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting by' looks like a phrase about surviving, but 'getting' is a link and 'by' is the multiplication sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The Times is a British national daily, and 'times' is the spoken word for the multiplication sign, as in four by two.

clue.text: Tedious jobs completed at last, OK with New York's redevelopment

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of this word

indicators.note: redevelopment rebuilds something into a different shape, so the letters it acts on are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Dull building jobs in New York are finally finished and approved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Completed at last' sounds like finishing the jobs, but it only supplies the final letter of 'completed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Donkey work is the dull, laborious part of a task, the drudgery left to someone like a beast of burden.

clue.text: Ministry of Defence's scooter squad

parts.note: MoD is the standard abbreviation for the UK Ministry of Defence
taken as written

explanation.surface: A defence ministry's unit mounted on motor scooters.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a military unit, but the department's abbreviation plus its apostrophe-s gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mods were a 1960s British youth subculture famous for riding Vespa and Lambretta scooters in groups.

clue.text: Excuse used before the advent of phone messaging

parts.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
a text is a message sent by phone

explanation.surface: An excuse people relied on in the days before mobile phones.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'before text' literally: the era before phone messaging is pre-text.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretext is a false reason given to hide the real one, which makes it a kind of excuse.

clue.text: Ate nothing around the end of June, then ate a lot

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: to fast is to go without food

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the month

explanation.surface: Someone starved until late June, then gorged themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface tells a story of fasting then bingeing; the opposite meanings sit in wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To feast is to eat a large, rich meal, so having feasted means having eaten plentifully.
